items.stem: In AWS IAM policy evaluation, what is the effect of an explicit deny?

options.rationale: Correct: an explicit deny always wins over allows in IAM evaluation.

options.text: It is ignored if an allow exists
options.rationale: Explicit deny takes precedence over allow.

options.text: It applies only to the root user
options.rationale: Explicit deny applies to all principals it targets.

options.text: It only works in resource policies
options.rationale: Explicit deny works in both identity and resource policies.

items.explanation: Correct: an explicit deny always wins over allows in IAM evaluation.

items.stem: Which TWO approaches follow AWS least-privilege guidance? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Grant only the specific actions and resources a task needs
options.rationale: Correct: scoping actions and resources is the core of least privilege.

options.text: Attach a permission boundary to cap a role's maximum permissions
options.rationale: Correct: permission boundaries limit the effective permissions.

options.text: Use Action:* Resource:* to avoid future changes
options.rationale: Wildcards grant far more than needed.

options.text: Share one set of access keys across the whole team
options.rationale: Shared static keys break accountability and least privilege.

items.explanation: Correct: scoping actions and resources is the core of least privilege.

items.stem: How should an application on an EC2 instance obtain AWS permissions?

options.text: Via an IAM role attached to the instance
options.rationale: Correct: instance roles supply temporary credentials without stored keys.

options.text: By hardcoding access keys in the code
options.rationale: Hardcoded keys are a major security risk.
Root credentials must never be used by applications.

options.text: By disabling IAM for the instance
options.rationale: IAM cannot be disabled; roles are the intended mechanism.

items.explanation: Correct: instance roles supply temporary credentials without stored keys.
